rows.textLatex: General Purpose Processor and Special Purpose Processor
rows.solution:
| General-purpose processor | Special-purpose processor |
| :--- | :--- |
| Open-ended processor that executes software for a wide range of applications. | Includes hardware selected for a particular class of work. |
| A general-purpose microprocessor commonly uses external memory and I/O to build the complete system. | The chip may include domain-specific computation or interfacing peripherals, reducing the external circuitry needed for the task. |
| Typical use is general computing and software-defined processing. | A DSP accelerates signal computations. A microcontroller integrates memory and peripheral interfaces for embedded control. |

note_ref.section: Processor categories, general-purpose architecture, DSP and microcontroller examples

rows.textLatex: Variants of Read Only memory and Read Write memory
rows.solution:
**ROM family.** Data is retained without power and ordinarily read during execution.

| Variant | Programming and erasure |
| :--- | :--- |
| ROM / mask ROM | Fixed contents. A mask ROM's pattern is set during fabrication. |
| PROM | User-programmable once. |
| EPROM | Electrically programmed. The common UV-EPROM type is erased using ultraviolet light. |
| EEPROM | Electrically erasable and rewritable, generally at byte granularity. |
| Flash EPROM | Electrically programmed and electrically erased in blocks. |

**Read/write memory (RWM).** Contents can be updated during normal operation.

| Variant | Storage and retention |
| :--- | :--- |
| SRAM | Uses a bistable cell. It needs no refresh while powered. Ordinary SRAM is volatile. |
| NV-RAM | Retains data without the normal power supply, for example by backing SRAM with a battery. |
| DRAM | Stores bits as capacitor charge, requiring periodic refresh. This trades refresh circuitry for higher density. |

note_ref.section: ROM and RAM families including mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash, SRAM, NV-RAM and DRAM

rows.solution:
| RISC | CISC |
| :--- | :--- |
| Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Uses relatively simple operations and generally more regular instruction encodings. | Complex Instruction Set Computer. Provides richer operations and generally more varied encodings and addressing modes. |
| Typically uses separate load/store instructions for memory and performs arithmetic on registers. | An instruction may combine arithmetic with memory access. |
| Simpler decoding helps pipelining. A task may take several simple instructions. | One instruction can perform several operations. Its decoding and timing can be more involved. |
| AVR is the RISC example in this course. | Intel x86 and Motorola 68k are the CISC examples in the notes. |

These are tendencies. RISC processors access memory through load/store instructions, and implementation determines the exact execution time.

note_ref.section: Instruction organization and execution. The notes’ absolute statements are treated as architectural tendencies.

rows.textLatex: Explain with appropriate block diagram the I²C communication protocol.
rows.solution:
**I²C** is a synchronous two-wire serial bus. The Mega 2560 uses TWI on PD1/D20 for SDA and PD0/D21 for SCL. Each line has its own pull-up. Open-drain outputs pull a line low or release it to let its resistor take it high.

```text
               VCC                         VCC
                │                           │
                R                           R
                │                           │
Mega SDA ───────┴────── target SDA         │
Mega SCL ───────────────────────────────────┴── target SCL
Mega GND ────────────────────────────────────── target GND
```

1. **START:** SDA falls while SCL is high.
2. The controller transmits the seven-bit target address and the read/write bit, MSB first. The receiver pulls SDA low during the ninth clock for **ACK**. A released SDA gives **NACK**.
3. Every data byte is followed by ACK/NACK. SDA stays stable while SCL is high during an ordinary bit. During a read, the controller NACKs the final byte.
4. **STOP:** SDA rises while SCL is high. A repeated START lets the controller continue without releasing the bus.

The notes identify the peripheral and pin assignments. See [Microchip AVR310 for the transaction sequence](https://onlinedocs.microchip.com/oxy/GUID-2BC8F654-C789-4AE6-809A-DA829B46B46E-en-US-2/GUID-1FC41A15-94E4-4480-9140-F8B528832554.html).

note_refs.section: Mega pin assignments PD0/SCL and PD1/SDA

rows.textLatex: Compare on-chip Timer and Counter of microcontroller.
rows.solution:
The same Timer/Counter hardware can run from either of two clock sources.

```text
Internal oscillator → Prescaler ──┐
                                 ├→ Source select → TCNTn → Compare / overflow flags
External Tn input → Edge detector ┘
```

| Timer mode | Counter mode |
| :--- | :--- |
| Clock comes from the oscillator through a prescaler. | Clock comes from rising or falling transitions on input `Tn`. |
| Each increment represents $N/f_{\mathrm{CPU}}$ seconds. | Each qualifying edge adds one count, subject to the counting mode and range. |
| Used for time intervals, delays and waveforms. | Used for event or pulse counting. |

note_ref.section: Internal clock path and external edge counting

rows.textLatex: What are the different types of interrupt signals available in a microcontroller? Write the name of timer flags that are directly associated with interrupt.
rows.solution:
**External interrupt requests** come from dedicated `INT0`–`INT7` inputs or supported pin-change groups. **Internal requests** include timer compare and overflow, input capture, ADC conversion complete, serial peripherals and the watchdog.

| Timer event | Flag in timer flag register |
| :--- | :--- |
| Counter overflow | `TOVn` |
| Output compare A, B | `OCFnA`, `OCFnB` |
| Output compare C on timers with channel C | `OCFnC` |
| Input capture on 16-bit timers | `ICFn` |

Each flag signals its event. The corresponding peripheral interrupt mask and global interrupt-enable bit must allow the ISR to run.

note_ref.section: Interrupt types, external requests and timer event flags
